newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuban dissidents will oppose one-party elections.
newsitem.headline: Cuban dissidents will oppose one-party elections.

text.p: A group of leading Cuban dissidents said on Monday it would urge Cubans to abstain from voting in the next round of one-party elections to be held on the communist-ruled island.

"We're going to campaign for people to abstain," Cuban political dissident Vladimiro Roca told a news conference in Havana organised by the Internal Dissidents' Working Group, of which he is a member.
Local government elections are scheduled to be held in Cuba at the end of 1997, followed by general elections for deputies of the National Assembly.
Roca said the polls held under Cuba's one-party political system were not real elections because they did not offer any kind of political choice.
He and other members of the Working Group called on the Cuban government to open a dialogue with internal opponents to save the nation from what they said was a crisis.
"Cuba is in a general crisis that is economic, political and social, a crisis that has to be resolved here inside the country," another dissident, Martha Beatriz Roque, said.
She said about a dozen opponents of Cuba's one-party government, including dissident independent trade unionists, were detained or harassed over the last week by Cuban police.

Roque said the Cuban government should stop presenting Cuba's problems exclusively as a dispute between the island and the United States. The real issue was between the government and the Cuban people, she added.
"The first thing we have to do is to start talking to resolve this peacefully," Roque said.

She and Roca were accompanied by other known anti-government opponents who are members of the working group, such as Rene Gomez Manzano and Felix Bonne Carcasses. The news conference was held at Roca's Havana home.

The dissidents said the aim of the group was to analyse Cuba's current social, economic and political situation and propose solutions for a peaceful transition to multi-party politics. Besides a call for internal political dialogue, the group proposed an amnesty for political prisoners, free elections and a multi-party political system.

Cuban authorities rarely comment on dissident activities or police action against it. The government routinely condemns internal opponents as "counter-revolutionaries" in the service of the U.S. government, which maintains a trade embargo against Cuba and seeks to isolate the Cuban government internationally.
Bonne Carcasses said the government had so far shown no sign of wanting to talk with internal opponents. "It's only intention ... is to stay in power," he said.
He added the government appeared to be "waiting for a miracle" to solve the country's problems.

The group's news conference followed a public statement last week by Cuba's president Fidel Castro in which he said he believed this year's sugar harvest, Cuba's strategic export, would fall short of last year's crop.

Sugar represents around 40 percent of Cuba's total exports and Castro's harvest announcement appeared to be a setback to the island's attempts to emerge from the economic crisis triggered by the collapse of trade and aid ties with the former Soviet bloc after 1989.
